strings.name: Barbara Liskov
strings.role: Programming languages and distributed systems researcher
strings.summary: Barbara Liskov studies how to organize complex software into understandable, verifiable modules. She led the development of CLU and Argus, advancing data abstraction and distributed programming. With collaborators she developed behavioral subtyping, replication protocols and practical Byzantine fault tolerance. Her work connects programming-language theory with dependable systems and earned the 2008 Turing Award.

strings.highlights.highlight-1.title: Data abstraction
strings.highlights.highlight-1.text: Led CLU, using abstract data types and modularity to support more reliable software.
strings.highlights.highlight-2.title: Subtyping and fault tolerance
strings.highlights.highlight-2.text: Developed behavioral subtyping and replication protocols with collaborators, linking language design and distributed-system reliability.
strings.timeline.event-1.title: Discussed replication research
strings.timeline.event-1.text: A published interview revisited modularity, state-machine replication and practical Byzantine fault tolerance.
strings.timeline.event-2.title: Computer History Museum fellow
strings.timeline.event-2.text: Recognized for practical and theoretical contributions to programming-language and system design.
strings.timeline.event-3.title: 2008 Turing Award announced
strings.timeline.event-3.text: ACM recognized her contributions to language and system design, data abstraction and fault tolerance.
strings.timeline.event-4.title: Named MIT Institute Professor
strings.timeline.event-4.text: Received MIT's highest faculty distinction while continuing work on languages and systems.
strings.timeline.event-5.title: Practical Byzantine fault tolerance
strings.timeline.event-5.text: Published PBFT with Miguel Castro to maintain services despite malicious replicas.
strings.timeline.event-6.title: Explored type hierarchies
strings.timeline.event-6.text: Discussed substitution requirements in abstraction and hierarchy, informing the Liskov substitution principle.
strings.timeline.event-7.title: Joined MIT faculty
strings.timeline.event-7.text: Moved from MITRE to MIT to study programming methodology and later lead CLU and Argus.
strings.timeline.event-8.title: Completed Stanford doctorate
strings.timeline.event-8.text: Earned a computer-science PhD under John McCarthy with research on chess endgames.
strings.timeline.event-9.title: Mathematics bachelor's degree
strings.timeline.event-9.text: Graduated from UC Berkeley, then worked as a programmer at MITRE and Harvard.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Born in Los Angeles
